strengths: Strong theoretical grounding: the paper proves (in a tractable linear setting) why post-training selection (PTS) and all-subspace learning (ASL) fail to recover Pareto-optimal submodels, and why nested subspace learning (NSL) provably does. This gives a principled justification for the design choice (nested training) rather than relying on intuition alone.

The central theoretical claim is empirically validated in a controlled, exhaustively-searchable setting (Fig. 2, Fig. 3), showing FLEXRANK recovers the true Pareto front that would require training all 10,000 submodels independently.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning both NLP (GPT-2, Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Llama-3.1-8B) and vision (DINOv3 ViT-L to ViT-7B) with consistent gains over strong low-rank baselines (SVD, DataSVD, ACIP) across a wide range of budgets.

GAR (Gauge-Aligned Reparametrization) is a useful, broadly applicable practical contribution that closes much of the gap between naive low-rank factorization and dense compute, with empirical validation of the theoretical FLOP savings (App. D.4, Fig. 10).

Thorough ablations isolate the contribution of each component: SVD initialization sample-size sensitivity, the necessity of end-to-end submodel training vs. per-layer training, and the importance of joint/nested submodel sampling vs. training a single budget.

The additive-error assumption underlying the DP rank-selection procedure, while acknowledged as a simplification, is explicitly stress-tested in App. C.3 with quantitative metrics (Spearman correlation, violation rate, DP exact-match rate, regret), lending credibility to a key approximation.

Good positioning against related work, including a detailed comparison table (Tab. 2) and honest discussion of a concurrent work, as well as non-rank-based baselines (LLM-Pruner, LayerSkip) for broader context.
Post-adaptation experiments (LoRA finetuning of submodels on math/code) demonstrate practical downstream usability of the extracted submodels, not just raw accuracy retention.
weaknesses: The theory (Sec. 4) is developed entirely for linear/bilinear factorization of a single matrix; its extension to deep nonlinear multi-layer networks is only heuristically motivated and validated empirically (small MNIST 4-layer network), leaving a meaningful gap between the proven guarantees and the actual regime (LLMs/ViTs) where the method is deployed.

For ACIP, the ablated variant without LoRA (i.e., essentially PTS-style selection) performs nearly as well as or better than the full ACIP with adapters, and is not drastically worse than FLEXRANK in some regimes (Fig. 4), which somewhat tempers the magnitude of FLEXRANK's advantage over the strongest existing baseline.

Training costs are non-trivial: the paper acknowledges roughly 2x memory overhead and 2x slower training than a dense forward pass due to teacher-student distillation and un-fused factorized layers, which is presented as an implementation limitation but is not addressed with actual optimized implementation results.

No comparison (even partial or on a small scale) is provided against architecturally elastic methods such as FLEXTRON/LLAMAFLEX or the concurrent nested-subspace work (Rauba & van der Schaar, 2026), despite both being discussed at length in the appendix/related work; the stated reasons (no public code, proprietary data) are understandable but leave the comparative positioning against the closest competing paradigm untested.

For the DINOv3/ImageNet experiments, only the classification head is finetuned while the backbone remains frozen at pretrained weights before decomposition; this simplifies the setting relative to the LLM experiments and may inflate the apparent robustness of FLEXRANK, since much of the network's representational capacity is not being actively adapted during elastic training.

Fig. 4 and Fig. 5 results (the main comparative results) are reported without confidence intervals, error bars, or multiple seeds, unlike Table 1, making it harder to assess the statistical significance of the reported gaps between FLEXRANK and baselines, particularly at extreme compression ratios where curves appear close.

The validation of the additive-error/ranking-preservation assumption underlying the DP procedure (App. C.3) is conducted on a small MNIST-scale network (4 layers, K=10), and it is unclear how well this generalizes to the much deeper, highly nonlinear Transformer architectures used in the main experiments, where the assumption is most heavily relied upon.
